utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. All the accused are here. Absent, Ms. Nikolic, Mr. Meek. The Prosecution, it's just Mr. McCloskey today. The witness is already present. Good morning to you, Mr. Butler. Mr. Josse will be proceeding with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour, and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this morning I would like to turn to the issue of your independent expertise. And on the 22nd of January of this year, at page 20158 of the transcript, my learned friend Mr. Ostojic was cross-examining you on this topic, and forgive me for saying this. He then got slightly waylaid on the issue of aerial images, and I would like to return to the subject without touching on that rather sensitive matter. And you had said to him that, and I paraphrase, with respect to the Srebrenica team and investigation, you accepted that you were integrated as a strategic member of the OTP. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Not of the OTP, but certainly a strategic member of the Srebrenica investigative team, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the transcript says that. I'm not going to hold you to that slight difference, because it's understandable, in particular because Mr. Ostojic speaks English so fast. But, anyway, leaving that aside, perhaps you'd tell us this: What was your role within that team; purely an analyst or did you have any other role?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: My role as an analyst was -- was primarily to help the team members, the investigators and the prosecutors, to understand the military context of the issues surrounding the crime base that they were investigating. I did not perform duties as an investigator in so much as interviewing witnesses and things of that nature. I mean, when I participated in those events, and I did participate in a number of interviews, I did so second chair, so to speak, to the investigator. They ran those types of issues that are within their competence to do, certainly. So my views, analytically speaking, with respect to where military units or police units were involved in various areas and time and everything else ultimately became part of the team's understanding of, you know, the larger issues of where military formations were and who their commanders were with respect to the crime base. So that was my role as an analyst. I was not a super investigator or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the interviews were concerned, did it ever occur to you to say to your bosses, "Well, perhaps I shouldn't participate in these. It's going to compromise my independence"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. In fact, the -- for me, the opposite was more applicable. Given the fact that much of my work, as I've testified, revolves around the fact of taking what was for formerly the JNA doctrine, the VRS documents and rules as I understood them, and because I wasn't a member of the JNA or VRS, I had a very keen interest in talking particularly those military officials who could provide information as to whether or not I was in fact pursuing a correct theory on the applicability of those issues. I mean, I felt that it was vital to my analysis to be able to get that opinion from these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you were present at the interviews of some significant characters, so far as this case is concerned. Correct me if I'm wrong. You were present at Trivic's interview, Sladojevic's interview, Momir Nikolic's interview, Borin's [phoen] interview and Erdemovic's interviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And bearing that in mind, wouldn't it be fair to say that you were Mr. Ruez simply with a military hat on? You've had a few years experience in the US military, you got to the rank of warrant officer, you did some analysis for the United States. What's the difference between you and Mr. Ruez? Why can't he give the evidence you're giving?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, going back to that particular context, Mr. Ruez, as a experienced police investigator and as the team leader, dealt with many aspects of the conduct of the investigation, which I would have had no involvement in; the issue of forensics, the issue of evidence collection, those types of things. I mean, those are not my area of expertise. I have no qualifications in them. Conversely, you know, as a police investigator and expert, you know, Mr. Ruez's limits with respect to being able to spend the months and in some cases years that I have spent looking at the military doctrine, understanding how the military interrelationship worked during the conflict, I mean, he would not have the ability to do that by virtue of a lack of the professional education to do so. So our roles are complementary and they're not necessarily overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So what do you put it down to, your education and experience in the United States Army or the very many years you had working for the very organisation that's prosecuting these seven men? What is it that you say allows you to come here and give expert military opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: It's a combination of both. My training with the United States Army gave me the knowledge and the tools to be able to understand what the job was and to know how to organise it to do the analysis, as I've had to do that in the past. My specific experience here, essentially working with, for lack of a better term, a non-public collection of material, gave me the specific expertise relating to this particular crime base and this particular military unit, the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How many warrant officers are there in the United States Army or how many were there at the point you retired?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. I could tell you that in my particular career field, as all-source intelligence analyst, there were, when I retired, roughly 150.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would the number of warrant officers go into the thousands?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, the warrant officer field in the United States Army probably would go into about, I mean, easily 25, 30,000.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps you'd help us. The correlation between a warrant officer and, shall we say, an officer who has just come out of the US military academy with the rank of second lieutenant is what, please? In other words, the lowest commissioned officer and a warrant officer, what is the correlation and the command structure between those positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Warrant officers, we are considered by -- in at least my military, we are considered to be our army's professional experts on technical issues. So in that context, that is why we exist. We are considered to be, certainly once you get to the rank of chief warrant officer two, you are commissioned, and in fact you take a commissioning oath. A young lieutenant coming out of the system, you know, these are young officers who will one day, you know -- are considered to be individuals who are also professionals in their trade and they will be groomed for command. As such, their professional education and professional development and career track, you know, are going to differ. By accepting the fact that warrant officers are not going to be individuals who are going to be groomed for senior leadership issues -- or senior issues of command, you know, we have the ability to be able to focus strictly on technical issues of our career fields and not have to, as we say, you know, be reassigned to other areas in order to broaden our perspective on various military issues that are of value to the service but not necessarily have any bearing to our own technical qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If push comes to shove, a situation occurs where there's a warrant officer and a second lieutenant, who's in charge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, the second lieutenant is in charge in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So -- and there must be tens of thousands of commissioned officers in the United States Army who therefore have command over warrant officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Literally tens of thousands?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, let's go back, if we may, to your role within the Office of the Prosecutor. You've described how you would give this, as you put it, technical expertise to the investigators and the lawyers. To what extent were you involved in constructing the case theory with the investigators and the lawyers, or did you step aside from that in order to maintain your independence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I -- I didn't see it as an issue of my independence. I was involved in setting up the case theory, with the -- to the extent that we were talking about the potential involvement of units of the Drina Corps and their subordinate formations. I mean, that was a fundamental component of my analysis, to be able to provide information which we would share with the investigators and with the lawyers that said, you know, here were the designated commanders at the time, here is the information that proves that they were in command during various portions. So, I mean, it was an integrated process. I mean, there wasn't an artificial separation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: To what extent were you party to discussions as to who should and should not be indicted before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe as I testified before, I was probably a party to almost all of those discussions while I was here. The difference is I just didn't get a vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the construction of the indictment in General Krstic's case; did you have any say or party -- or part in the construction of that indictment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: In the sense of General Krstic, I was certainly involved in the construction with respect to the factual issues that went as part of the indictment. I don't believe I was involved with respect to issues relating to, you know, legal issues, theories of liability, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You had your part and your say in the construction of the factual allegations that that man faced when he stood trial in this building; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about when it came to Colonel Blagojevic and I think it's Major Jokic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, to the same degree. My responsibility as part of that process was to contribute with respect to the factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And clearly perhaps most importantly, what about in relation to these seven gentlemen who are standing trial here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Pandurevic was indicted as part of the same package that General Krstic was, so certainly I was heavily involved in the indictment of Colonel Pandurevic. I think there was -- I was involved to a certain degree with Colonel Beara, Colonel Popovic, because I believe the discussions on those individuals was still occurring while I was here. With respect to Generals Gvero and Miletic and Colonel Borovcanin and Drago Nikolic, I don't believe I was involved, because I think most of the substantive issues behind that may have already occurred either as I was getting ready to leave or as I was leaving, so I don't think I was heavily involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right, let's move on. I'll ask a matter of a little sensitivity. What about the unfortunate victims and all their families of these awful crimes; have you had any dealings with them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, not -- not at any level I'm aware of. I mean, I would have obviously come across them with respect to, you know, their testimony as witnesses and things of that nature, but on a professional investigative basis, other than maybe meeting, you know, once or twice, you know, someone like Hasan Nuhanovic, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the wives of some of the men killed; did you ever meet any of them in the field, inadvertently or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I know that I may have come across the testimony of one or two, again, as part of the witness process, but, you know, as a general practice, dealing with the actual victims was not something that I needed to do or deal with to do my work, so I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you have conceded that you are not independent of the Office of the Prosecutor, for the reasons you've described, but you have maintained that you're entirely objective. That's really what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, as a practical reality, you know, I acknowledge that I'm not independent of the Office of the Prosecutor because I worked for them. Having said that, you know, my understanding of what my role is within the organisation, as an analyst, is to be able to, to the extent that I can, demonstrate what ground truth was, and it has the impact that it has on where the Office of the Prosecutor takes cases. That is why I've tried to do as detailed a job as I can in footnoting and making clear all of my particular judgements and conclusions, you know, because I am aware of the fact that I'm not going to be perceived as a neutral party.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you think the maxim "he who pays the piper calls the tune" has any application in your case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Again, as I indicated before, as a matter of my professional training, my military superiors expected me to be able to give them the most candid and truthful observation of what was happening on the battlefield, obviously despite my own loyalty to my own army. That's what I was paid to do, that's what I was trained to do. I did it in the United States Army, and to the best that I could, I did it in the same location for the exact same reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to upset the United States Army, so I'm not going to ask you about your role there, but I am going to ask you about your role here and try and test what you have just said. Give the Trial Chamber one concrete example of where you stood up to your bosses in the Office of the Prosecutor and said, "No, I don't think that theory is right because of X, Y and Z," in relation to the military field. Demonstrate your independence to this Court.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: You've -- you could probably subpoena half of the Galic trial team, to include the Deputy Prosecutor of the OTP, and get an entire chapter on my disagreement with how the Office of the Prosecutor dealt with the Galic case. I was one of the two military analysts assigned to that, and I think that if you polled the second floor, you probably would get most of the senior trial attorneys who would be able to tell you in chapter and verse how bloody that fighting was with respect to military opinions versus prosecutorial goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how did that manifest itself in the trial, for those of us who don't know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, at the end of the day, it's the responsibility of the senior trial attorney to make the decisions for the conduct of the trial. Perhaps the best thing that can be said about that is the fact that after the Prosecution case was over, I was no longer working for that particular trial team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this aspect of your independence you've just described, did it manifest itself at all in the Srebrenica team?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: To a large degree, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because there was no disagreements?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: The thing which made it very professionally rewarding for me in the Srebrenica team, and what set it apart from the Galic case, for that matter, was the fact that from the very beginning, the investigative team did not have a preconceived notion of who they were going to indict and how it was going to work and then tried to make the analysis fit. They were very receptive to the idea -- to the fact that collectively at the time, we all didn't know. I mean, I think I've testified that the Drina Corps when I got here was an abstract entity. We didn't know what it was and what it meant, and it was a collective process where we all came to, you know, the knowledge base together. So it wasn't a question of trying to jam military analysis in order to fit a legal theory. It was more along the lines of the fact that the legal theory was built around the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back, if I may, to where I began. I've nearly finished this line of questions. You are saying that what distinguishes you from Mr. Ruez or, for that matter, Mr. McCloskey are the years of experience you had in the US doing military analyst work and the fact that you were able to devote so much time to military issues when you came to The Hague; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You accept, don't you, that if it wasn't for the fact that you'd had all this time to examine these particular matters, you in fact wouldn't be in a position to comment on these matters, over and above thousands of other members of the US Army, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My expertise is based on my work. I know we've had this discussion on a legal basis about what a military expert is or is not, but I can assure you that other than CNN, you know, nobody has the title "military expert." You know, your expertise is developed on the basis of your history, your training, and the work that you do, not that you go to a qualification course and you walk out as a military expert who can talk about any particular region under the sun.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But it would be fair to say, wouldn't it, that you couldn't comment about practicalities in combat in the way that a person who actually served in combat could? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I would disagree, in so much as I have done a number of contingency and combat-related tours, and I understand that. That's my job to understand that. I mean, the United States Army trains me to do intelligence, you know, in the clear light of the fact that it's going to be done in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How can you comment in the way that, for example, an officer who had senior command of a unit in combat would be able to, bearing in mind the events that you're dealing with here, with real fighting, real flesh and blood, I'm afraid?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, sir, I would go back to, again, as a role of the training and experience. The United States Army, and my knowledge of the British Army, you know, they don't take experienced combat commanders off of the line and say, "Well, today you're going to be my intelligence officer," or, "You're going to study logistics." You know, the fact that I'm not a brigade commander, you know, is precisely why, you know, my army trained me to understand how their brigade commanders work, an opposition force. I don't have to be a brigade commander to understand that. I do the research. I don't have to be a professional logistician to understand how an opposing force's logistical train should work. We don't use our logisticians to do intelligence. We use our logisticians to supply our army. That is how we operated. That is the course of my training and experience. So I understand your position, how can I comment on what a brigade commander was or was not supposed to do with respect to the rules and his training because I wasn't one, but, you know, the opposite is that because that is precisely what I was trained to do as part of my own military profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your lack of practical experience of combat makes you very ill-equipped to comment as an expert, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: You may have that opinion, but I will disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's -- let me ask you one last thing. Shortly after the passage that I referred to at the beginning of this morning, the learned Presiding Judge tried to cut through things in "a radical way" and asked you about how you understood your role as an expert. And you commented that, and I'm paraphrasing here at page 20159, that you weren't an independent arbitrator of the facts who had no association with the OTP, but you believed the way your reports are written and information is provided, that you're being as fair and as technically accurate "as I can with the assistance of the Court." You're bound to say that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: That is -- that is my role as an analyst. I'm bound to say a lot of things. I don't quite understand the question. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at what I suggest --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- is you betray your objectivity and you showing your bias towards at least one of these accused. And If we could please have in e-court the VRS Main Staff command responsibility report. I'm told I need a 65 ter number. 2764. And we need to go, please, to paragraph 2.10. Now, this was the report that you wrote dated the 9th of June of 2006 in relation to the Main Staff, and the passage that I'm taking you to is the passage that deals with the assistant commander for morale, legal and religious affairs. And after saying that the sector was an important component of the Main Staff, you say: "First and foremost, this staff element was responsible for managing the information/propaganda campaign in support of war aims." That's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You are saying that the main role of that sector was propaganda, rather than morale, are you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Propaganda is a tool by which people use, you know, information in order to impact morale. It's -- it's a component part of how it's done. It's not a separate issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That may be right, but first and foremost, that sector dealt with morale; propaganda may have been part of the issue and import of morale, but what you should have said there is that they dealt with morale, not propaganda. You said "propaganda" because it sounds worse. That's the truth, Mr. Butler, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I guess I don't -- I don't put the same meaning or connotation to "propaganda" that you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, why don't you describe in that report anywhere anything else about morale other than propaganda?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: The issue of morale, while an important part of military operations, I mean, doesn't play into the issue of what happened in July of 1995, as far as I can determine. I mean, the fact that the staff section is entirely involving itself -- to a large degree, I should say, not "entirely," you know, involving its issue to maintaining the positive morale of the soldiers of the VRS and, to a larger extent, also the RS population behind the war aims, is a fascinating military issue that has very little bearing on July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You're making it up as you go along, Mr. Butler. Read 2.10. There's no reference to 1995, is there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, okay. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to put my case forcefully to this witness, and I'm entitled to do that, in my submission. And if my learned friend feels he needs to be a hound dog and guard dog for this gentleman, then so be it, but I am going to put my case firmly and squarely to him. If the Court thinks I'm exceeding the bounds of propriety, then they'll tell me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and we're telling you precisely that. I don't think we should -- you should use such words as, "You're making it up as you go along, Mr. Butler." Please, you can make your point and get there using more moderate language. All right. I mean, please keep in your mind that not everyone is used, familiar to the kind of cross-examination that you are used to, and that some people happen to be more sensitive than others and some people would understand the words or the phrase that you used in a way which is very offensive. I don't, but I think it's the case of moderating.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll heed the warning, thank you. I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 2.10 does not deal with 1995, does it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, but the whole context of these reports, as I've indicated as a component part of the introduction of these reports, is that they ultimately deal with issues of 1995. So I've said it up front. I hope I don't have to repeat it in every paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, for example, to test what you've just said, why mention at all, then, the issue of the military prosecutor's offices, bearing in mind they had ceased to be a responsibility of my client from mid-1993? What possible relevance did that have?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: The possible relevance of that is even though General Gvero's office ceased to have control over that process, the fact that that process was still available to him, first of all, in July of 1995. The second part and why I believe it's relevant is that going back to the October 1992 guidance, where the -- his particular branch, you know, sends out the information in a correct manner, reminding the senior military officials of the army what their obligations are, and at the time he was sending it out, he also controlled that as well. So, for me, it's a framework of establishing the fact that by position and not just by his own, what, over 25 years of military experience, that these are issues that he should have been acquainted with and in fact was acquainted with in 1992. So that was the connection that I am trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you accept that the concept of morale, using the word "concept" reasonably advisedly, connoted and involved a great deal more than information/propaganda?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the reason you didn't say that was because you say it had no relevance to the events that concern this case; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, just going through the issues of morale, for example, under the issue of morale, how soldiers who are killed serving their army and their country are dealt with, their military funerals and the benefits that the army provides with that respect, particularly in the culture I understand it, is of enormous significance, and the particular morale branches of those units were deeply involved in doing that correctly to honour the families and the service members. It's an important position, but in the context of what we're talking about in July 1995, is not of particular relevance. By not mentioning it in that context, I'm not saying that it's not an important factor. It certainly was. But for the purposes of why we're all here today, it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you this once again. Let's look at the sentence: "First and foremost, this staff element was responsible for managing the information/propaganda campaign in support of war aims." Bearing in mind your concession that the sector was involved in much more than information and propaganda, do you think that sentence was misleading?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely not, sir. I mean, the reality is that most of the soldiers in the army did not, one, have a vested interest in the creation of an independent state, they did not have a vested interest in the ascension of power of Radovan Karadzic and the SDS, and that they were fighting for their own simple goals of the protection of their families and the protection of their villages. So the efforts of the VRS, in order to try and reach out through informational campaigns, through propaganda, through whatever means necessary to try and impart shared goals and shared values on a largely apathetic group of soldiers was of enormous importance to the army. And I think from very early on, the senior leadership of the army recognised that as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I think it's arguable whether you've answered my question, but I'm going to move on and invite you to consider the answer you've just given, because it's an interesting answer. And you might want to read it back. It's an answer that comes from someone who has expertise in matters political rather than military, isn't it? Isn't it a good example of your straying over the boundary and really simply saying whatever suits the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm saying what's in a reflection of the military documents that I've read. I mean, I don't need to be a political expert to understand the ramifications of the 1993 Banja Luka military mutiny and issues related to that. I don't need to be a military expert to understand what General Mladic is saying in military publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Butler, but none of us need to. The reason you're here is not to help with things that you don't need to be a military expert about. You're here to help specifically with military matters, and that answer belies that, doesn't it? That answer shows you're straying into matters of politics and media and propaganda, different areas of expertise. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, because the issues that I'm talking about revolve around the conduct of how the VRS operated, I mean, which is a fundamental component of why I'm here and what, as a role -- my role was in the office of Prosecutor, understanding how that worked and why it worked the way it did under various circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In this case, we haven't heard from a media expert, but media experts have been instructed by the Office of the Prosecutor, haven't they, in other cases?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I won't say that you're wrong, I just -- I don't know. I don't know what you qualify as a media expert, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that's what we said in the case that I was involved in. Be that -- be that -- be that as it may, you wouldn't accept that the issues contained in, if we turn the page, 2.11 of this report really matters that are better dealt with by someone who has political, media, or even perhaps expertise in the area of propaganda?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, only so much as the fact that my views on these matters are a direct reflection of my work with the VRS military documents. I mean, if an outside expert wants to come in and spend three years reviewing this in the same manner for these same types of insights, I'm certainly -- you know, it's something that can be done. But my expertise on this and what I've written in this particular paragraph is a reflection of my understanding of what the VRS was saying in its own documents about its own goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I just pick you up on what you just said? It really did take you three years or more to get to this state of knowledge to be able to give this type of expert evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Probably considerably more than that. I started the process in June of 1997, and as I think I indicated to Ms. Fauveau yesterday, you know, every day I still learn something new about this particular case. So, I mean, I've been working on this now over a decade, and I'm not going to say that I'm even close to approaching the peak of knowledge that I hope to one day have on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's look at the last paragraph on this subject, 2.12, please. Would you accept that all the warring parties were engaged in disinformation to some extent?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why do you say that the sector for morale was itself involved in showing increasing sophistication throughout the war in relation to disinformation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think -- and again my reflection of reading their documents is that in the early part of the war, their view was that the Western media was particularly biased against them, in substance and form of reporting, and their initial inclination was to deny access to much of that Western media. As the war progressed, the VRS leadership came to realise that cutting off the media in that respect was actually being more counterproductive and that what they needed to start engaging in was a process by which they could start to offset the negative media by allowing select access to Western media or by offsetting it by media outlets that they viewed to be more sympathetic to their views. So part of it is potentially, you know, the socialist culture of being able to completely control the media, and then here these professionals are where they don't have that and they start to recognise, you know, the ramifications that an independent media and independent reporting, as they called it, was having on their war aims and how their operations and war aims were being viewed by larger communities. So they did become more sophisticated over time in their efforts to structure information that was being put out by these media outlets in a light more favourable to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My question was specific and related to the sector for morale, rather than the VRS --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: The sector for morale controlled access of the media. It went through them in the Main Staff and through the corps. So they were the leading edge of being able to control that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But the matter was largely in the hands of the politicians, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Not with respect to the armour, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, but largely, insofar as the outside world was concerned, it was the politicians, it was Dr. Karadzic who was controlling it. Don't lay the blame at my client's door. Be fair.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Again, my views on these issues are shaped by the VRS military documents that I've read. They reflect that the VRS itself believed that it had a role to play in this process and did so. Whether or not it was subordinate to Karadzic or superior to the politicians is not a matter that I looked into.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at another aspect of this paragraph. You say that the activity of disinformation reached a zenith in 1995 when UNPROFOR and later the Rapid Reaction Force were seen by the VRS leadership as significant obstacles to their objectives. Well, the Rapid Reaction Force was undoubtedly a significant obstacle to the objectives of the VRS; we can agree on that, can't we?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I mean, certainly from their perception.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that's why General Smith wanted to create that Rapid Reaction Force, in order to obstruct the Bosnian Serbs; it's as simple as that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I believe General Smith has testified to that. I don't -- I didn't follow all of General Smith's testimony, so I can't tell you what he would have answered with that. I mean -- so, I mean, I don't know the answer to that. I mean, I assume General Smith was asked and answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's examine UNPROFOR, which is General Smith as well, in fact, because of course he was the commander of UNPROFOR. But from your perspective as a military expert, UNPROFOR were posing significant obstacles to the objectives of the VRS. You admitted that yesterday in relation to the Srebrenica and Zepa zones, the enclaves, not policing them properly.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So all you stated there is the obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I mean, "obvious" is a point-of-view argument. My views on that, again, are with respect to what the VRS was saying about the UNPROFOR in their own documents. Whether, in the light of a neutral review by somebody, the UNPROFOR was or was not neutral is not an issue of relevance to me. What is an issue of relevance is the fact that the VRS believed that the UNPROFOR was tilted against them and that that was a planning consideration for them and they took it into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So you're saying it's not for you to say if that was fair on their part or not; you're just saying it's a fact of life that it's something that they, the VRS, took into account? That's the tenure of your evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you also end with the lovely word "obscured," the true intent of the VRS military objectives obscured. It's not surprising that the VRS military objectives were obscured. Most, if not at all, military objectives are obscured in some way, are they not, particularly in wartime?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and -- you know, just like -- you know, I don't mean for the phrase "obscure" to have some sort of a sinister connotation. You know, the fact that the VRS would want to hide its true military objectives from outside observers, to include the UNPROFOR, is a natural consequence of military actions. I don't see that as a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll be stopped if this is a rude or unfair question, but haven't you deliberately structured that paragraph, which states, for the most part, no more than the obvious, in a particularly pejorative way so it sounds and reads badly for General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I guess I have to confess that even though we share a common language, your view of it and mine are radically different. No, I don't see it that way at all, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't have views, Mr. Butler. I'm simply putting a case to you and asking you some questions. Let me make that clear.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I would disagree. I don't believe that I have structured this in some form of a sinister view, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. We'll return to the report in a few minutes' time in relation to one other aspect. I would like now to turn, if I may, to my client's presence at Pribicevac and the document P849. It's 849. Yes, that's the right document in e-court. Now, you gave evidence, in relation to this document, what seems to many of us, and I suspect this includes the Trial Chamber, an eternity ago on the 16th of January, 2008, at page 19794, and you were asked what you can tell from the fact that it was directed to Gvero and Krstic personally, and you comment on Krstic and then you say: "General Gvero, the Main Staff officer, is present at that location as well." And you in no way qualified that. You simply said that it shows that Gvero was present as well. That wasn't always your opinion, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: My understanding of what General Gvero was doing there was, as I've discussed before, it was rather a common practice for the Main Staff to send out an officer --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: -- to do that, I mean, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to stop you because I --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: If my opinion has changed on that, I mean, you're obviously free to show me, because I think I've been fairly consistent through the years on what General Gvero was doing there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was only stopping you because we are going to turn to what he was doing there in a few moments' time. I'm not going to avoid that issue. The issue that I'm first asking you about is whether your evidence has ever shifted on the issue as to whether in fact he was there and --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Oh, okay, whether in fact he was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give you an opportunity, if you want, before --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: It -- it may very well have. I don't believe initially -- I don't believe initially that we had visibility that General Gvero was there at the time. I think it was only through some latter documents that came out that his presence was established at that location. So, I mean, it wouldn't surprise me that my view would have changed on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, it did, because in the case of General Krstic, at page 4823, you were asked this question by Mr. McCloskey: "Now we have General Gvero. What can you make of his presence on this document?" And your answer was as follows: "This part for me, analytically speaking, an unanswered question. We have no physical evidence or we have no other information, either from sightings or from any other aspect of our information, that indicates that General Gvero was physically on the ground at Srebrenica or at the forward command post. There are a lot of ways to read this. I mean, he could in fact be there, and this is the only indication that we have of it, and I cannot confirm that or that this message was sent to him at the Main Staff for his benefit as well. But the short answer is, relative to General Gvero, I don't know." Now --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I remember that passage, and, yeah, at the time that was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what is it that's made you change your mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I believe that subsequent to that, as part of the continuing investigation, a number of officers from the VRS, you know, have in fact, you know, reflected that he was there during this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: So, I mean, that tends to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. So I would accept that, that based on what various people have said in the eight years since you gave that evidence, it's been suggested by a number of witnesses, not all of whom were in the VRS, for your information, in fact, that he was present at that command post at that time. Why didn't you say that? Why didn't you qualify the answer, because it's quite an important point, isn't it? And let me explain the point to you and put it to you. Your analysis of the document didn't reveal that Gvero was there. You were quite clear about that in the Krstic trial. The only reason you're giving support to my client being present there is based on what other people have said in the intervening period. Why didn't you say that? Why didn't you make it clear the nature of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe that I did. I don't -- again, as I discussed before, I wasn't in the habit or practice of putting witness base testimony into the context of my reports, but certainly where I'm asked these questions in court, you know, I can wrap that particular issue in, and I do as part of my oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you didn't, Mr. Butler, you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: At that point in time, I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Apologies. Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You didn't -- when you gave evidence before this Chamber ten days or so ago, you simply said: "General Gvero, the Main Staff officer, is present at that location as well." You didn't seek to qualify that by explaining that you make that assumption, that conclusion, on what others have said and not on the basis of the document. It belies your trade is what I'm saying to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's the second time he's misstated the evidence, as if this document has nothing to do with the presence of General Gvero. It's improper to misstate the evidence. It creates a chaos in the record and it creates confusion in the witness. The witness should not have to identify when a lawyer misstates the evidence. It is a fundamental principle that I -- I'm sorry, that I need to object to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I agree with that, but how am I misstating the evidence? I don't understand the objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey's suggestion is that the document itself has nothing to do with this or cannot be used as a basis reading -- it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, with respect. I simply don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said: "This is the second time he is misstating the evidence, as if this document has nothing to do with the presence of General Gvero." This is precisely what he is alleging that you have misstated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It must be my fault. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. You asked the witness to explain why, in making the statement that he made to us some ten days ago, if I remember well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Shall I try again, Your Honour, and see if I'm misstating the evidence? I'll try again, if I may. Perhaps I didn't make my point or my question clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me find your question, because I think the question was clear. You said: "You didn't -- when you gave evidence before this Chamber ten days ago, you simply said General Gvero, the Main Staff officer, is present at that location as well. You didn't seek to qualify that by explaining that you make that assumption, that conclusion, on what others have said and not on the basis of the document."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's been explained to me, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You're saying, are you, Mr. Butler, that you make the conclusion that Gvero was present based on the document? I think that's where Mr. McCloskey is saying I'm misstating the evidence. Is that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I'm trying to unravel this in my own mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't read Mr. McCloskey that way. I don't know. Perhaps Mr. McCloskey can explain further or perhaps we can -- but I didn't read Mr. McCloskey as meaning that. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler has testified he's always taken the document into account and he's also now taken evidence into account. To pick one or the other and suggest it's the only reason why Mr. Butler has come to a conclusion is a misstatement of the evidence, in my view, and it's an important point. Otherwise, I wouldn't have bothered. But to suggest, one way or the another, that his opinion is only based on the document or his opinion is only based on the evidence, is improper, because as I view it, his questions have incorporated both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we can safely move, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the document is concerned, the document alone, you presumably stand by what you said in Krstic's trial --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- document alone in isolation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: In isolation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what you're saying is in this court, your evidence needs to be read in conjunction with what other people have subsequently said? I think we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and to expand on that point, the whole purpose of my narrative reports, and in the past trials as well, you know, need to be looked at in the light of what other witnesses and what other individuals have said on these issues. I don't want my reports to be taken in isolation for precisely that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And my question is a simple one. When you gave the evidence ten days or so ago, why didn't you say that? Why didn't you say, "It's not based purely on the document, it's based on oral testimony, statements," whatever, as well? That's what I'm exploring.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, sir, if I recall the question correctly as you recited it, I wasn't asked to explain why I know, and, you know, I have been encouraged to some degree to be as brief as possible with my answers. Certainly, had the question been asked, and it has been asked by you, I'm willing to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And are you able to say offhand who the individuals are who've made you change your mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe that it was -- one was, in fact, General Krstic. I believe that the OTP interview of Obrad Vicic, the operations officer for the Drina Corps, also confirmed that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Anyone else? Anyone who's given evidence in this trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Nobody strikes me as someone who's given evidence in this trial, so I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. I promised we'd come to the second part of the evidence in relation to that, and that is your analysis of Gvero's presence there and having any significance. And you went on to say: "No, sir, other than just, again, a reflection of the practice where in critical operations, that often officers of the Main Staff will be present at these command posts to help oversee the operations." And you go on and expand upon that. Do you have any idea now where General Gvero came from prior to arriving at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea where he went when he departed the IKM?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe that at some juncture, he arrived back at the Main Staff headquarters, because we have him in intercepts and in orders, I believe, on the 11th and 12th. But, I mean, if -- from where he left and where he went after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So based on that, how can you conclude so confidently that the reason he was there was to oversee operations on behalf of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Okay, I see. Then maybe this is where context is useful. When we normally talk about General Gvero's involvement, particularly with respect to previous trials, a fundamental component of the Defence of General Krstic, particularly, was that General Gvero was in fact there as some form of a manifestation of an independent chain of command around the corps commander. When I talk about the issue of General Gvero's presence there, you know, as the Main Staff representative, it's -- it's in light of the fact that he's performing his function as the Main Staff and that he is not somehow usurping the responsibility or authority of General Krstic as the chief of staff and later commander at that juncture. So that's -- that's how -- you know, the context by which I address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I invited you to give that particular answer, but what you're saying is you're basing your analysis, in effect, on what Krstic said in his own defence at his own trial; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. What I'm saying is that normally when the issue of General Gvero comes up and what his purpose is, that is -- that is one of the main reasons that colours that. My analysis of what General Gvero is doing there is on the basis of what General Gvero's role would have been as a Main Staff officer and the customary practice of the Main Staff to send these people to these forward locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But that is ultimately speculation; you don't know what he was doing there, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, and I know that. My role -- my view of what he was doing there is coloured by his role as a Main Staff officer. I don't have the specific document that articulates why he's there and exactly what he's supposed to accomplish there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My last question on this: Bearing in mind what you've said, from my point of view, rather helpfully in that last answer, I don't want to be unfair, but why didn't you say that when Mr. McCloskey asked you the original question, because the an important qualification, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Sir, I believe I have said that, when I was asked what he was doing there, and I explained what he would be doing there in his role as a Main Staff officer within the custom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you don't actually know that; it is ultimately speculative on your part, so --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, it is a presumption, yes, sir. I don't know, as a fact, exactly what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I mean, I assume he wasn't there in a lounge chair, but I can't tell you that, you know, his role, you know, on the basis of any specificity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I'll settle for that and move on. The next issue I'd like to turn to, please, is the order purportedly from General Gvero of the 13th of July, and that can be found at P45. And simply bring that up for a moment so we can remind ourselves of what I'm talking about. I'd like to briefly look, as a preamble to the questions about the document itself at what you said about it in your Main Staff report at page 24. So could we have the Main Staff report up again, please, which was 2764. And it's 4.9. I'll let you read the paragraph to yourself, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we blow that up? I can't read that very well. I don't know if the witness can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's why I've got my glasses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it good like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm fine, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can read it, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You don't give there the detailed analysis of the document that you have in your oral testimony. Any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I'm noting there the context of the order. If you want to read back my oral testimony on it to refresh my memory, it might be helpful, and then I can explain, you know, or answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, in essence, you deal there with the fact that -- your evidence that Gvero was competent to issue the order and also that it was a broader reflection of the cooperative effort of the generals of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's summarising it. Why didn't you put that in the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: In this context, I mean, it was something that I didn't know that was going to be an issue brought out in court as part of my testimony. This part of the report, it's just kind of time-lining issues through. I didn't put that there. I mean, I thought it was fairly self-evident that that was part of the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What, that it was within Gvero's competency, one, and, two, part of the collaborative effort of the Main Staff; you took that as read, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir. I mean, the documents that you showed me on the issues of unity, command yesterday and those laws, as a matter of practice that, you know, because we're talking about professional military officers, many decades of experience in some part, you know, I -- I operate under the general working assumption that, you know, as military professionals who understand the importance of these issues, that they're not going to be issuing orders that are outside of their competence to do and that at the Main Staff level that these officers are not going to be engaged in some kind of guerrilla campaign to undermine their own authorities, the authorities of their fellow officers, or the goals set by General Mladic. So that's why I make those statements in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a moment, if I may. Briefly on this paragraph itself, two things. Firstly, it says "finally directs the Main Staff be kept informed of ongoing activities ..." In fact, the document says that the Corps Command and the Main Staff should be so informed. Any reason why you didn't put that in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, that is something that, as you've just noted, should have been something that should have been in the report, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And the other point, arguably equally pedantic, at the same sentence you talk about interim combat reports. The actual document - and it might be worth getting it back up on to the screen, but perhaps you'll take this from me - says "send interim reports with specific details of the situation," et cetera. There's a difference, isn't there, between an interim report and an interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't take it as such. I believe that they're one and the same type of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's break that down, if we may. Is there a difference, in your expert opinion, between an interim report and an interim combat report? In other words, isn't there a type of report which could be called an interim report which is not necessarily an interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: If there is, I'm not -- just not familiar with it. I mean, in almost all of the contexts that I've seen the phraseology used, it's always "interim combat reports."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And a follow-up from that is: Notwithstanding the answer you've just given, why did you add the word "combat" into your report when it isn't in the actual document? Do you want to have a look the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, I mean, I take your word for it, and I guess the answer would be, like I said, it's a phrase that I've long been accustomed to using, it's one report and it's generally referred to as interim combat report. If it is your position that there are in fact two different types of reports, one of them is not -- is an interim report and a combat report, I mean, I would like to see that, but, I mean, I certainly will hold that open as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's have the document on the screen, please. That's P45. Could I have a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one, you're going to have to zoom up a little bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were being asked questions by Madame Fauveau, and in the course of an answer, you're talking about General Tolimir, in fact, and you say: "You know he is aware, like everyone else, that, you know, General Mladic is the commander of the army and he's not going to give orders in contravention to what General Mladic wants accomplished." And then you added: "We see this with people like General Tolimir. We see the same situation with people like General Gvero, who are given what are presumed to be operational orders that, at face value, one would think they shouldn't be giving because of their specific role." Now, it's right, isn't it, that certainly at first blush, when we look at this order, one wouldn't expect it to come from the assistant commander for morale, religious and legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, that in the title "Assistant Commander for Morale," et cetera, the important word was "for"? In other words, what he had to do was look after morale, religious and legal affairs; that was his portfolio within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it goes without saying, as you've already conceded, that this order fell, certainly at face value, outside the remit of that particular job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you also concede that General Gvero had limited operational experience, probably none that you're aware of, anyway?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I disagree, sir. I've read the translation of his military records, and he had a -- over a decade, at least, of operational experience as an infantry officer before assuming his next, you know, part of his military career and the political side. So I disagree with your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And when did that cease?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Oh, boy. I think probably by the -- and again, you know, I think we have the documents, I hate guessing, but probably by the mid-1980s he was focusing much more of his career on the political work side rather than the operational side. But, I mean, he is and he remains -- until he became a general, he remained an infantry officer by career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps at the break we could get Mr. Butler that document so that his refreshed recollection to answer the question is more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I couldn't agree more. Shall we have the break now? Is it convenient for you, Mr. Josse, or do you wish to finish this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, it is convenient. Because also this is, I'm afraid, my longest topic, but I'm doing well time-wise, I can tell the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good, nice music for our ears. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. McCloskey has been very helpful, if I might say. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He always is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we can go into private session on this subject at first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You want to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's what he said. He didn't have his microphone on, but that's what he just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I thought I had heard that, but let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me show you this, Mr. Butler, and see if this is what you're referring to. I will give you the B/C/S version of the record card, plus the part from 1980 that has been translated. If you are, in the answer you gave just before the break, alluding to a different document, perhaps you'd let us know.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I think we're on the same track with this. There is -- on the B/C/S version, there is the material from the 1970s as well, but I think we're all on the same page of data here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right, in which case I'll deal with this shortly, and I hope not to make a mountain out of a mole hill. Let's put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: The English or B/C/S version, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, English, I think. Would you agree with me that from 1980 onwards, there is no operational experience on that record sheet?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I certainly agree that by 1980, it looks like he has tracked into political and legal affairs as his main career focus. Maybe it's -- and in my mind, a definition of "operational," when I see him performing duties at 2nd Corps in Titograd, I see that as operational, but as I certainly agree that by 1980 he is spending most of his career focus dealing with issues of the political and legal affairs branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be a case of semantics, possibly important semantics over the use of the word "operational," but this is completely different sort of work that would be done in the staff section of the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know that I can say that as an absolute fact, only because I didn't do a whole lot of in-depth research on the political office or process in the JNA, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Well, so far as the document prior to 1980 is concerned, unfortunately, as I've already said, we only have that in B/C/S. Let's put that on the ELMO. Whilst that's being done, you think you've seen an English translation of this, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. I think my view of it is off of the B/C/S one as well. I don't believe I've seen an English translation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And this isn't --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: This must be something else, because I wouldn't have -- there's something else out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you know what my next question was going to do, which is: How were you able to interpret that? Can I put my case to you? My case is that General Gvero was the commander of a platoon in 1963 and thereafter was not involved in command-type work for the rest of his career.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: (redacted) he was an infantry branch officer and held the normal suite of infantry jobs for approximately the first 12 years of his career, which I believe in one of them is a company command. But I certainly concede that after that 12-year or 13-year mark, he spent most of his career dealing primarily with the issues of the political branch and did not continue to follow the mainstream track of an infantry officer with respect to a battalion command or a brigade command. So, I mean, I think we're good on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this, but can we go into private session again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Butler, before the break, I was asking you about the 13th of July order, and we were going through various aspects of General Gvero which related in some way to the order. The next issue I wanted to ask you about was something we touched on yesterday, and that's the subordination principle. Bearing in mind the subordination principle, again, on the face of it, the order was outside his competence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, from my view of it, it certainly looks like an order that would have more appropriately been type-signed by the chief of operations as opposed to Colonel Gvero -- Colonel -- General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And in the answer that you gave Madame Fauveau yesterday, you talked about presumed operational orders, in the plural, that at face value one would think they shouldn't be giving. Can you think of any other example like this in relation to Gvero?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: During this particular period, I don't believe so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any other period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: To be honest, I haven't -- I haven't gone back and looked for similar types of orders in 1993 or 1994 or even early 1995, so I just don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, looking at what was happening at the time, there is no question that the VRS perceived that they faced a serious threat; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Matters undoubtedly required expedition? In other words, the instructions, the orders, call it what we will, needed to go out to the subordinate command expeditiously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And there might even have been, within the ranks of the VRS, dare I say it, even within some of the Main Staff itself, a sense of panic at what was happening with the column; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Certainly by 13 July, there was a growing awareness of the military threat of the column. I wouldn't call it "panic" at that point. Maybe that sets in a few hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. Let's have P45 back on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we look at the top of the document, and for this purpose the original B/C/S will be fine, if not better, we can see that it says: "Strictly confidential number," and then it says "03/4-" and then there's four digits. "03" meant what, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: My understanding of the numbering sequence is that the "03/4" was the numbering sequence used by the operations shop for its orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The number of the morale sector was "07," wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I'll take your word for that. I mean, I think you're correct, but I just can't recall with certainty. But it sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What significance, if any, in the context of this document, do you place on the fact that it says "03"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: As I believe I've testified, if not in this case, certainly in other cases, that I believe that this -- the contents of this document were drafted by the operations people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And bearing that in mind, what reason do you think they would have got Gvero to sign it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Again, as I think we discussed yesterday with Madame Fauveau, I mean, since I don't know the hour-by-hour whereabouts of General Miletic, I mean, one of the assumptions that could be made is that General Miletic was temporarily unavailable to sign it. The bottom line is that, you know, I don't know what the motivation was of the operations people to decide that this order needed to be issued under General Gvero's name versus General Miletic's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You said helpfully in your evidence-in-chief that the document had not been signed, as such, by Gvero. It certainly has his name at the bottom. There's absolutely no dispute about that. The fact that the two letters "SR" don't appear on it has what significance, if any, to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Again, I think we've all noted that it reflects the fact that it wasn't personally signed by the individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's also right, isn't it - I'm sure there's no dispute about this - that very soon after receiving it, General Zivanovic at the corps level basically sent the order out again to his subordinate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and in fact, in large degree, it's because of that issue is why, when I look at this and while it makes for an interesting discussion on why General Gvero's name would be on it, you know, I think that given that the people who drafted it didn't seem to have any particular difficulty with it, and certainly the people who it was intended for didn't see this as an unusual type of occurrence, that there was no question about the fact that the people involved, that this was -- you know, the fact that General Gvero's typed signature block is on this order was somehow irregular or improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as that is concerned, what about the reverse point, that when Zivanovic receives it, he thinks to himself, "Hang on, this is strange. It's come from Gvero. Gvero has no authority to send out this order. I'd better send it out again under my name," because it clearly makes sense and it's clearly important, "so there is absolutely no doubt that it has proper command authority"; in other words, a complete reverse to what you've just said? Isn't that likely or equally likely?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, sir, if it were a one-time occurrence, it would be.
