Having said that, given that there's just such a large body of these types of things where an order will come in from superior command and then effectively be regenerated by the intermediate command, the corps, and sent down to the lower brigades, that I don't view it as such. And, you know, my issue on that would have been, is that General Zivanovic would have been the first point, on receiving this order, that if he had that type of a question, it would have been incumbent upon him to inquire back to the Main Staff, if this were something that could be issued under those particular circumstances. And I don't believe there's any information that says he did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you've just said that my theory, for want of a better word, would be okay if this was a one-time occurrence, but this was a one-time occurrence, wasn't it? I don't understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. I think when you look over the context of orders that are coming in from various organisations within the VRS, from the Main Staff to the Drina Corps or other corps, for that matter, and then with the corps sending those out to the brigades, it was generally a practice where those intermediate headquarters would essentially -- in many cases they cut and paste these same contents or guts of a directive and put their own header information over it and sent it down. So, again, as part of that much broader review of material that I've done is where I say I don't see this as a one-off issue, I see this as a consistent practice in most respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But it wasn't consistent so far as General Gvero is concerned. You've said that a minute or two ago.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. Yeah, most of the situations that I've seen, it would be coming under other individuals' signatures. Like I said, I haven't gone back and looked at Main Staff orders specifically with respect to General Gvero on this, so I do hold open the possibility that this may very well be the first time that General Gvero has done this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think we can agree, can't we, that this would not have been sent by whoever without General Mladic's approval? You've said that in your evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: My evidence -- whether or not he specifically approved this, my -- my thrust of the discussion is the fact that this isn't going to be sent in such a way that anyone could conceive it as being in contravention of what General Mladic ultimately wants. It's going to be issued in the context of that and it may very well be the fact that it is directly based on instructions he gave. It's not going to be counter to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: THE COURT REPORTER: I'm sorry, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm beginning to think it's just me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. At beginning of this thing I told my colleagues that you had given me some piece of good news during the break, found the solution to the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I know that you, like yesterday and before, you will be doing your utmost -- we'll be patient and -- THE COURT REPORTER: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay now? I am still not -- yes, yes, it seems to be okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume I need to re-answer the question for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see first whether we have the full question: "I think we can agree, can't we, that this would not have been sent by whoever without General Mladic's approval. You've said that in your evidence-in-chief." You didn't add anything to that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So you can now proceed with your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And again, as I discussed I believe in my evidence-in-chief, while I don't know that General Mladic may have specifically directed this to be sent out in such a way, it is that -- you know, that it's not going to be in contravention to what General Mladic's views are on the situation and what his overall goals are. So it's not going to be General Gvero or any general on the Main Staff, for that matter, issuing orders that are in contravention to those decisions by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, would you exclude the possibility that this order was sent out in General Gvero's name without him actually knowing of its existence at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I can't exclude that as a possibility. I mean, while as a matter of military professionalism an officer is supposed to know what orders are going out under his name, I certainly can't prove as a fact that he did know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got two small issues and then one slightly longer one, and then I'll be done. The first of the small issues relates to Colonel Djurdjic, who you referred to in your examination-in-chief at page 19725. You were asked by Mr. McCloskey who, in your opinion -- I'll read it as it reads in the transcript: "Who is your opinion of who Djurdjic works for, if you can tell?" And your answer was: "I believe the documents that I see in Colonel Djurdjic is a Main Staff officer. I'm not sure at present whether he in fact worked directly for General Gvero or worked out of the operation shop for Colonel Miletic." In that regard, could we please have in e-court 6DIC149. Now, Mr. Butler, whilst this is being brought up, let me tell you what it is. You will immediately recognise the diagram or the schematic. The addition to it was made by General Skrbic on the 18th of September of last year when he was giving evidence before this Chamber, and it's the short -- the little addition that I want to ask you about. There it is. We can see that other than his signature and the date, he has added, next to the commander of the Main Staff, "AK," and that "K" was "K" for "Kabinet," and in effect he was saying that in parallel with General Mladic, there was a cabinet or an office which was involved in running the Main Staff. And I'm not going to ask you to comment on that quite yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can we go to the next document, which again was used by Madame Fauveau in her cross-examination, which is 5D431. And we'll need to go, please, to I think the second page of that in both English and B/C/S. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We can see that this is a summary of duties of units and establishment elements, and at the top we've got the commander and his aide-de-camp and then after that we have something which is described as Kabinet, with a "K," in B/C/S, translated as "office" in English. And beneath number 4, we see: "Foreign military representative liaison department," and underneath that, the chief. And that, we suggest, is Colonel Djurdjic, and that's where we say he fits into things. In other words, what I'm putting to you, and I know this is a long question, is that he was part of the cabinet of the commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, yes, sir, and again while it is inconsistent with the information that I've seen, certainly this raises that as a valid possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question perhaps which you can explore with -- or one matter which you can explore with the witness, Mr. Josse. I see that against that "chief" under number 5, there is a code which is exactly the same as that next to "chief" under 3 under "office," so could we be talking -- does the fact that the two code numbers are identical mean that we're talking of the same person, or could we have two different persons having the same code reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is that question directed to me or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am not putting the question directly. I'm asking Mr. Josse whether he wishes to explore this with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad to say I'm not in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you help, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I'm afraid not, sir. I would have to look at this document in its whole context. I notice, going down there, there's another "chief" that's listed, and it has the same particular code as well. So I don't know if it has a direct relevance or not. I mean, so far -- on the B/C/S version, I'm seeing three with that same code numbers, and I can't possibly believe it would be the same individual trying to hold three positions. So the short answer is: Probably not, but I really would have to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Krgovic has gone to take some instructions, and perhaps I could be given a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The way I see it - but of course I may be wrong, and the witness can help us further if he is in a position to do so - is that for a chief in whichever area of duty it occurs, the code number is what you see on the screen, that's "110001". That's how I understand it, because wherever it occurs, you have "Nacelnik," and that's "chief"?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact what I -- I can help a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same way with "adjutant." Obviously, the phrase "adjutant" is there three times and it has three code numbers as well, so I mean--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So that's what I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I suggest to you that in fact the chief of the cabinet was a man called Banduka [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I have heard that name associated with -- while it's called cabinet, we call it -- basically it's the commander's personal staff. I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, just going back to the answer you gave a few moments ago, you said that it is inconsistent with the information that you've seen. What information is it inconsistent with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have a -- a version of the Main Staff -- a working roster of that organisation where the names of individuals are penciled in at various points of time, how long they've been in that position, and where it fits within the organisational structure. I have a copy of that in my hotel room with the notes. I believe this is a document that Ms. Fauveau and I had talked about before. I guess I will add that to my shopping list of material to bring at the end of court today for your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. The next issue relates to P3025, which is the Krivaja-95 document. Could we go to page 4 in the English, please, and it's going to be page 3 of the B/C/S. The very bottom for the B/C/S. English, middle of the page. We see that it mentions here, as part of the targets, "open fire on observed targets in the sector of the Potocari school," and then it mentions a number of other places. And you were asked, at page 19783: "And these target lists that they give, do you have any reason to believe that any of those are either civilian or UN targets?" And you say: "Yes, sir, I do. I believe the facility known as the 11th March Factory was in fact one of the buildings that the UN was using." Now, a few points. First of all, isn't -- wasn't that factory outside of the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But your understanding is, nonetheless, the UN were using it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe, like I said, this is an issue that the investigation had looked at and determined that there was either equipment being stored there at some point for the UN, so that's the basis of my decision, that I understand it was. If in fact that's not the case, then certainly I'll stand to be corrected on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was it in fact targeted, that factory?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe that question was raised at some juncture with the individual concerned, Captain Mico Gavric, who was the artillery officer for Bratunac. I'm not sure what his answer was. I believe it's a component of the Blagojevic case so -- I don't believe that I'm aware of any direct information that shells were hitting it, but I'm not, again, sure whether or not -- whether Mico Gavric indicated that it was shelled or at least targeted. So, I mean, I don't know the answer to that offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the school is concerned, could we go to page 2 in the English and page 1 at the bottom in the B/C/S. At the top there, we see the suggestion that the 28th Division reserve, I'm paraphrasing, "is stationed in Srebrenica, the village of Potocari (the school)." So it does appear on the face of this document that it was the belief of the VRS, or at least the author of this document, that there was a military component at the school?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Any idea whether the school in Potocari was actually targeted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't know, sir. Again, it's been a while since I've heard Mico Gavric talk about it, so I just can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on, if I may. You were asked in your evidence about 6D207, which was a document purportedly from General Gvero to the Drina Corps headquarters, and at page 19800, in the course of your evidence-in-chief, I'm going to paraphrase this I hope fairly by saying, in effect, you said that what the VRS were saying here is: "People from the outside the International Community are looking at us. Let's make sure we put our best face on."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's a fair characterisation of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Gvero sent this very soon after a rather fraught conversation that he had with General Nikolai; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Correct, sir, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And that conversation with Nikolai, certainly common sense would indicate, had a significant causal effect in him sending out this warning; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: It may very well have. I mean, I won't disagree with that. I mean, I don't know the -- the answer, but it certainly is a plausible, you know, explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You're in effect saying that this was put out not so much for show, because of course it was an internal document, but to make sure that VRS subordinates, corps and brigades, presumably, would behave in a way that would be seen as acceptable by the International Community? In other words, it was a rather cynical document is really what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not saying it at all, per se. What I -- what I believe I've testified about this is the fact that, and again what we discussed earlier this morning, it was a legitimate military interest for the VRS to be perceived as acting fairly in this regard. And, again, particularly with this document, you know, I highlighted the fact, I believe, that at the time that General Gvero is sending this, his superior, General Mladic, is orchestrating threats against the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You did -- I want to be fair. You characterized it as "a good military idea."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so I certainly don't want you to get resolved --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I think this illustrates exactly what we were talking about this morning, that, you know, it isn't eye-wash; it is the fact that General Gvero inherently recognises the value of this towards the aims of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Right. And there are other documents that we can find in the vast array of documents at your disposal which indicate VRS commands telling subordinate units to obey international humanitarian law, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You can go over them, but I agree, I would say there are multiple references.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to go over very many, but perhaps we could have a look at P414, which is the combat analysis document of 1993. Page 59 in English. No, it's 414. It's a very large document. And this extract, I'm sure you'll take it from me, is in section 2, which is the part that deals with the assessment of the morale of the Army of the Republika Srpska in 1992, so it's from the morale section of that report, which itself is quite large. Page 53 in the B/C/S. And we see here it says: "In contacts with UNPROFOR, ICRC representatives and those of other humanitarian organisations and of the media, establish correct, measured and civilised relations befitting the military and perform the duties professionally with mutual respect and appreciation." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to take what you've said, Mr. Butler, your helpful remark, at face value and save some time. You have said a few moments ago you can go over them, but I agree there are multiple references.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, from 1992 onward, there are multiple references that VRS senior officers understood the importance of adhering to the law of war throughout the course of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Finally, and on a similar note, could I ask you to have a look at two photographs, which is 6D193 and then 6D194. Now, 6D193 is a photograph of a commemorative plaque, dated 13th of August, 1996, that was given to General Gvero by Michael Walker, a British general. And if you turn it over, on the other side is the actual plaque. I don't know whether you've become aware of this in the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This hadn't -- wasn't something you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: It wasn't hit by the radar scope --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: -- no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And 6D194, take from me, was a bottle of whiskey signed and presented to my client by a Major General Wilcox, another British general. Both of them were with the -- it says there the Ace Rapid Reaction Corps, which was the succession of the Rapid Reaction Force in 1996, so this was just after the war had ended. In your exploration of this unfortunate war, have you come across multiple examples of UN generals giving gifts to the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: It was relatively a common practice. I mean, one that stands out, of course, in my mind and I believe many people's is, you know, the rather playful picture of General Mladic and General Clark switching hats around. It happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And why did it happen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I -- I couldn't begin to explain that, that one. I mean, how they're going to interact with each other as part of their liaison professional relations, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because you were never in that position, isn't that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- is that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I was not in a position to be doing that type of stuff, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's why you don't know, is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's fair enough. And the fact that these gifts were given after the war, in other words, there was far less reason for the giver of the gift to in any way try and curry favour with the recipient, any significance in that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: You know, I don't know. I mean, I have heard many anecdotal stories, again particularly with the focus of the VRS, because that was the American sector, and their very high thoughts about what they saw was the professionalism of the VRS where they were and that this type of practice did occur, but, I mean, I don't have an opinion one way or another on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And as you've already explained, you've -- do you have any specific awareness in relation to this particular case, have you come across it in relation to any of the other accused either in this case or indeed in relation to the Krstic case, or anything that you specifically have investigated or analysed yourself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. More time-consuming than probative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse, and thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just finally this in relation to it: You're saying this doesn't surprise you at all, that General Gvero received these gifts from these gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he said it, he's not surprised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I've got nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just give me five minutes to get physically set up and take over from Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If it's even more convenient for you or if you so wish, we could also have the break now, and then you start and continue until quarter to 2:00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, that would be fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Agreed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's what we will do. We'll have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Butler. I'm the last of the magnificent seven, and as you can probably tell, another Brit.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I won't hold that against you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm glad about that. In May of 2000, when you wrote your first Srebrenica military narrative, can we take it that the -- you had reached a state of knowledge that the Drina Corps was no longer an abstract entity to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that at that point in time, you felt sufficiently well-appraised of all the documents you had by then seen to draw the conclusions that you did in that report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to place matters into context, by the time you signed off that report, General Krstic's trial had been underway for about two months; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I thought it had been a little bit longer, I mean, but again my memory may not be clear on that. Two months sounds --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It probably doesn't matter, Mr. Butler. You knew the trial was underway?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sir, the trial was underway before I signed off on it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you at the time you signed off the report appreciate the purposes for which that report was going to be used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Namely, that it was going to be used as evidence to convict General Krstic of the most serious offences imaginable?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I knew it was going to be used as evidence in court. The issue of guilt or innocence was not something that I was making a consideration out of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to get into an argument too early, but you knew you were going to be called as a Prosecution witness?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you knew your evidence was going to be used to support the indictment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: The form of that report has been put to you as historical. Was that a report the form of which you had ever written before in your prior career as an intelligence analyst?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have on occasions been asked to take a static point in time and to essentially deconstruct it and to explain it as a part of my role as an intelligence analyst, so I have done that on occasion. It's not my primary purpose, which of course is more a predictive issue, but it's something that I have engaged in in the past, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that was the point I was seeking to make, but I'm not going to labour the point. In terms of the content of the report, I want to see if you agree with my assessment that the military narrative report really contains four categories of information, and I'll list them for you, and you tell me whether you agree. Firstly, there is unattributed prose; secondly, there is prose which is directly referred to a footnote; thirdly, there are quoted sources, for example, the rules of the brigade; and, lastly, there are phrases placed directly inside quotation marks or, as you may say, parentheses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean -- I mean, I -- "prose" versus "text" may be a semantic, but, I mean, yes, I believe what we're talking about is the same information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I assume that in placing phrases inside quotation marks, your intention is to reflect the fact that you are directly quoting from a document or other source.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you were good enough to tell an advocate earlier in the case that you had been heavily involved in the preparation of the case against Vinko Pandurevic, my client?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'm not sure you did tell us this. At what point in time did that become part of your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, the preparation of the case, you know, it's always been my responsibility with respect to, you know, analysing the information and related to that. I think that if I get the thrust of where you're going on this, is at a point in time, and I believe it would be probably around summer of 1999, if I have it correct, is when the state of the investigation and the material that we had gave us an initial read on the first three individuals that, you know, the decision was being made might have potential criminal liability, those being General Krstic, Pandurevic and Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So certainly by the time you signed off the report of May 2000?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I'm not -- as indicated, the Pandurevic indictment was approved internally by the Office of the Prosecutor and, I believe, then sent to -- you know, for confirmation by one of the Judges at the same time as the Krstic one. So, I mean, that was the initial series of indictments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to complete this little chronology of the report and your involvement in various people's cases, you testified in the Krstic case on the 17th to the 21st of July, 2000, a couple of months after you signed off the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, if it was 2000, I'm -- I'm just trying to remember offhand. I don't exactly recall whether we -- when we actually did the indictments, whether it was the summer of 1998 or the summer of 1999, so I'm a little bit fuzzy on that. I just -- but, yeah, I do recall testifying in the summer of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, as somebody who, like me, is heavily involved in the case of Vinko Pandurevic, I'm sure you'll agree that one of the, if not the most significant documents in his case is the interim combat report of the 15th of July, our P329?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you'd also agree that it's very important that anybody trying to determine his guilt or innocence gets a full understanding of his meaning in that document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that is a document which you sought to interpret not only here in evidence but in your narrative report of May of 2000; that's right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll suggest to you at the outset that the critical phrases in that report are pregnant with ambiguity and give you the opportunity to comment on that now. Would you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I would disagree, and my basis for disagreeing is that, you know, having gone through this issue of ambiguity and parsing of words, my foundational position is that, you know, military documents, written by military professionals, are written for clarity and so that there are no misinterpretations of the meaning, so that's usually my foundational position on these issues. It means what it says, but certainly I will hold open your, you know, comments on ambiguity, and I expect you'll ask me about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, to cut straight to the chase, I'd like to ask you a few questions and see whether you agree with me about, as it were, the context in which the document was written, before we come to the precise words of the document itself. And if you don't mind, can we move to a couple of days after the document was written, the 17th of July of 1995, and that is the day after the so-called corridor had been opened and many thousands of enemy soldiers, many of whom were armed, had been allowed to walk free to the free territory by Vinko Pandurevic; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And as you told Mr. McCloskey, this had been done in direct contravention of orders of superior command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And on that day, the 17th of July, the brigade -- the Zvornik Brigade, that is, was visited by three colonels from Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the purpose of their visit was to investigate why an order of superior command had been disobeyed by Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to put that visit in context, throughout the prior 24 hours we've seen several examples of disingenuous behaviour by Vinko Pandurevic towards his superior command as to what he was doing and what in fact he had done?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that characterisation of his behaviour. I don't know that it matters for where we're going, but I don't believe he was being disingenuous. It may very well have been a function of the fact that, you know, he made the decision, hadn't been able to fully brief his superiors at that point, but I don't think there was ever a design that he was trying to deceive them about what he did. And in fact he made it clear later on exactly what he did and why. So, I mean, I don't agree with your characterisation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Prior to the opening of the corridor - and I will come to this in another section of my cross-examination - would you agree that there is evidence of frequent communications between Vinko Pandurevic and enemy forces, with a view to negotiating the passage of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: There is -- there is much information out there, and I believe Dusko Vukotic was a part of that, I believe that PW-168 discussed that to some degree as well, that certainly on the Muslim side, they were trying to forge an agreement with Colonel Pandurevic to let the column through. But, you know, throughout the 15th and at least the early morning hours of the 16th, Colonel Pandurevic felt he had the military means to continue to resist the column and did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is it within your knowledge that the negotiations were conducted throughout the day and the evening of the 15th of July, before and up to the point at which the irregular combat report of that date was written?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't have an exact timeline of when they were going on. I mean, I certainly believe that by the 15th, the Muslim commanders are talking. They may have even been talking over this issue as early as the 14th, before Colonel Pandurevic got there. So I take what you're saying. I just don't know it as a fact. But it wouldn't surprise me if it were that early.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, did you, during the whole of your seven years' attachment to the Office of the Prosecutor or at any time previously, ever have the opportunity to listen to tape-recorded conversations between Vinko Pandurevic and Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. If they exist, I didn't listen to them. I mean, I don't know whether they're in the possession of the OTP or whether they're in possession of ABiH Army, so, I mean, I did not listen to the context of those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever during the course of your seven years employment at the OTP or any period since then have access to witness statements or interviews with members of the 28th Division who'd passed through in the column?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and at one point I remember early on talking with Semso - and I'm going to butcher his last name. I apologise in advance - is it Mutanovic [phoen] or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think if you just call him "Semso," we'll know who you mean.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I did talk with him and he had indicated that. But at the times of having that discussion with him, my own basis of information wasn't sufficient that I really understood what he was really trying to get to. So, I mean, I was aware that there was a -- you know, talk back and forth between Colonel Pandurevic and others of the Zvornik Brigade and the members of the column to negotiate this, but it wasn't an issue that I particularly focused on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So when you give your opinion as to any meaning of the irregular combat report of the 15th of July, it is ignorant, as it were, of the exchange of information between them that might have dealt with their respective military and humanitarian positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, again, going back to what I've said before, it's not a question of not knowing about it. Whether or not it's in the detail that I may have liked to or not, it's the fact that given the position that, you know, what happened with the column was a military act, it wasn't a particular issue of relevance, the negotiations back and forth, with respect to what happened along the crime base. So that's why it didn't receive perhaps as much attention as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not for the last time during the course of this cross-examination, I'm going to refer you to some evidence which you may have now appraised yourself of, namely, the evidence of PW-168 before this Trial Chamber. He agreed with these two propositions: That by the evening of the 15th of July, two things were obvious; that in order to avoid massive loss of life on both sides, the soldiers of the 28th Division would have to be let go; and, secondly, that Vinko Pandurevic's superior command were never going to give him an order to do that. Does that affect your opinion as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But here we must be careful, Mr. Butler. Does the information that you have available to you cause you to concur with his assessment of the situation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that the documents that we had and we have in our possession to this date does correspond to that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want there to be any ambiguity here. I'm suggesting that that was the position by the evening of the 15th of July, at the time the irregular combat report was written.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Like I said, I mean, the documents correspond to the general situation. I cannot say, obviously, as a fact whether or not that the witness is correct with respect to what Colonel Pandurevic recognised at that juncture. I mean, I just -- I don't know that. I can confirm that the documentary evidence that's out there does dovetail with the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well, then. Let's turn to your interpretation of this document. And can I make a couple of very simple points first. You're not the author of our P329, the interim combat report of the 15th of July, are you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: You're asking me if I wrote the combat report; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not write the combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you haven't spoken to the man who did write it, have you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I agree, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So your interpretation of this document is not based on any knowledge of what the writer had in his mind?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, sir, certainly during the proceedings with respect to the first two trials, I agree with that. There were -- and maybe I shouldn't do this in public session. Maybe this might be more appropriate in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll just jump into private session straightaway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in private session, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just -- again, not knowing the full background, I mean, I understand that at some point in time, there were contacts between the Office of the Prosecutor and then General Pandurevic where there were discussions related to his potential surrender to the custody of the ICTY. And, again, while I wasn't a direct participant in those, one of the issues that did come up was, you know, I did become aware of information with respect to the explanations that Colonel Pandurevic gave for that particular document. So, I mean, I certainly have that in mind when I get to this particular juncture in time. So that's all I needed to raise. I don't know whether it was appropriate to do that in public or private session, sir. I apologise then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we could have done it in public session, if you agree to change the status of that part of the transcript. I don't know. Mr. McCloskey, I don't see any problems with the Prosecution. We've heard more or less the same evidence before, and I think it was in public session so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that part of the -- this part of the transcript will become public. We can revert to open session now and proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, and thank you, parties. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just to clarify that last answer, there's no mystery about what you're talking about. You're talking about an investigation report that deals with a conversation or an interview over the course of a meal between an investigator on a different team called Eileen Galice and my client, Vinko Pandurevic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: In part, but there was also a series of conversations related to the potential negotiation process of a surrender that weren't part of that particular issue, and that's why I -- that was the other part that I was thinking of, because I know that there was some sensitivity at the time pertaining to the Office of the Prosecutor and those contacts with the accuseds, so that's the other part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. But you can't possibly have known about them in May 2000, when you signed off this report, can you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, and that's what I said, that's why I structured accordingly what my state of knowledge was at that time during those proceedings and then what it is at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And even after May 2000, did what you read in the investigation report from Eileen Galice impact at all on your interpretation of this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, sir, it did impact in so much as that as part of Rule 68 obligations, it was an issue -- you know, his interpretation of what that phrase meant or what he was talking about was an issue that we had to explore, because it was, you know, a potentially exculpatory issue. So it did impact me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that at any stage in your review of this document, you have sought to use it as exculpatory material in the case of Vinko Pandurevic or, indeed, anybody?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I haven't sought to use it as such, because I don't get into the issues of whether, you know, it's exculpatory or not. My view is, you know, I interpret the document based on what I understand at the time. There is, to some degree, a difference of opinion between myself and others, you know, with respect to its legal value, I mean, so, I mean, that's why I just stick with what it means in the context of the military issue, not what it means in the legal sense or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, before we actually come to looking at the document, I want to revisit something you said to Mr. Josse yesterday when you were dealing with your understanding of the Serbian language. In your evidence-in-chief, you told us that the Serbian word "asanacija" has been translated by the CLSS as meaning restoration of the terrain and that you understood it to mean the process by which biological, human, animal waste and things of that nature were removed or buried?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Or disposed of on the battlefield, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does that phrase come from the military lexicon or is it, as it were, an expression that you, together with the CLSS at this Tribunal have, to use a better word, compromised on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: It is my understanding that it does come, and if memory serves, it was actually we pulled the phrase right out of the JNA lexicon, and it was an exhibit in the Krstic case, so everyone was quite clear what it meant. So I don't think I'm attributing a different meaning to it. I mean, we did bring the meaning forward before the Court because we did recognise that particular terminology issue existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And forgive me, did I understand the drift of your evidence correctly that the difficulty with that particular word meant that the irregular combat report of the 15th of July, in translation, went through a number of drafts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I think the difficulty with that -- and I don't know if that was the first document where it was used. The difficulty wasn't with -- at multiple revisions. I believe the difficulty was that from an English language perspective, I didn't feel that the euphemistic phrase of "restoration of the terrain" somehow conveyed the right context of the fact that what we were talking about was, you know, in a technical state, you know, burying biological hazard products, human and animal wastes, and that's why, I mean, as a matter of just trying to keep the record as clear as possible, we endeavoured to actually put the definition before the Court so we wouldn't get into an interpretational battle. It meant what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you look at other documents other than the military lexicon in translating this unusual expression?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't believe so. I mean, the JNA lexicon gave what I believe was an adequate definition. I know that somewhere along the line, we did come into possession of a JNA document which was dated 1974, if memory serves, that talked about medical and veterinary processes on the battlefield, and I think we actually did check there and came up with essentially the same definition. So, I mean, I didn't think we went any further than that. The issue seemed to resolve itself in the Krstic case as to what the definition meant. Nobody essentially disputed it, and we moved from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to finish on this particular aspect of your involvement with the CLSS, was it the case that you were in consultation over how the English translation of this document should be produced or what it should look like or what it should say?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. I -- I don't get involved in stuff like that at all. My involvement was strictly revolving around the phrase that, when translated into its literal term, didn't seem to make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if we can put our first document into e-court. It's 7D480, please, and we'll start with the first page of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Definitely a newer version than I've seen before, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You haven't seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, not this particular version. This is a much more recent document than -- than I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We've had this translated by the CLSS, and, I mean, you can look straightaway and see that their 2008 translation of this document is quite different. They translate "asanacija" as hygiene and sanitation measures, rather than restoration of the terrain. Was that how the 1974 document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's apples and oranges. The term was "asanacija terena [phoen]," and so -- and I don't see that on this. And grilling Mr. Butler about, you know, words such as this, I think the definition should be -- or the word should be correct. The term we're talking about is -- in the document is "asanacija terena."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to come to that. Mr. Butler has told us that the phrase "asanacija" means restoration of the terrain, and I'm going to come to why there's a "terena" in that sentence. So that's an you utterly false objection, and I'll carry on. I'm merely showing him the front of the document so that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe that that's -- was what Mr. Butler said. That may be the way it's being interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we should continue this discussion in the presence of the witness. I think if there is going to be a discussion, it won't be in the presence of the witness, but I think we can -- having heard you both, I think we can proceed. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go to English page 5 and B/C/S page 6 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, is that sufficiently enlarged and focused for you to read it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and I appreciate that because I've noticed I've left my glasses in the room, so that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You and I both have the same problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment. The B/C/S and the English pages that we see do not correspond. The B/C/S starts with paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the B/C/S probably needs to go back a page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, no. No, I still don't think we are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, in that event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are there now, we are there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we -- yes, zoom in, please, that's correct. And start with 1. Yes. Okay. Your question, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just read, really, the first two paragraphs over to yourself. You said you saw a much earlier document. Was it in similar terms to these as to, as it were, the general provisions of hygiene and sanitation measures in battlefields?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, this is the same -- in general terms, this is the same type of process that they are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And so under paragraph 2, the process that you were talking about, hygienic and sanitation measures, included the following: Finding the wounded who were accidentally left behind, gathering them, giving them first aid, and evacuating them into medical institutions; finding, gathering and helping wounded or deceased animals or animals that were accidentally left behind and, if necessary, evacuate them. I'm going to stop because somebody is trying to attract my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, I don't read the B/C/S language, but now, even comparing the two texts, it's obvious that they do not correspond. For various reasons. If you look at paragraph 1, there's something missing in the English translation. Paragraph 2, it's not subdivided into the various bullets in the B/C/S, so I don't think we are looking at the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to suggest a practical measure. If I carry on reading it slowly, we can cure the problem in e-court later on, and then the translators can do their best to let the accused know how this document translates back into B/C/S. But for present purposes, I'll read paragraph 2 and pose a question to Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if we go to the previous page in B/C/S, we are there. Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly looks like it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is, that's it. Thank you, Madam Usher and Madam Registrar. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And carrying on: "Finding, gathering and (burying or burning) those who have been killed and establishing the necessary records; finding, gathering and removing (burying or burning) or using animals carcasses; gathering and eliminating (burning or burying) all kinds of waste dangerous to the health of people or animals; catching abandoned (lost, stray) animals, gathering military property and personal belongings of wounded military personnel (or military personnel who have been killed or who have died of natural causes)," and so on. And did your understanding of the term mean that it included, as it were, the recovery of the wounded and the treatment of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, my understanding of the term did not include the treatment of wounded in that broader phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So in your view, when you wrote your report of May 2000 and you interpreted the irregular combat report of the 15th of July, you were predisposed to the view that "asanacija" could only be carried out once a battle was over; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir. My view was that the phrase "asanacija" was -- that we were talking about was resulting in the issue of burial of biological waste, human or otherwise. It didn't reflect on to whether it occurred before, during, or after battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, forgive me. Then that must mean, seeing a document that now describes to you that it includes the recovery and treatment of wounded, that you concede you had a fundamental misunderstanding of the term when you wrote your report, mustn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I believe the term as it's used in that report is referring to the activity that was occurring on the ground. I mean, we can parse words all we want on this, but you have to look at it in context to the overall situation, and we can talk all day about what it could have meant, but when we are confronted with a large body of information that's saying -- or that's indicating exactly what it was, you know, it could have meant recovering the wounded, but there's absolutely no information that suggests that it was. It could have meant digging -- burying animal carcasses, but there's no information to suggest it was. It could have been gathering straight military property, but there's no indication that that's what it was. So, I mean, we can play the word game, but I think that you have to ultimately, when you look at these military documents, look at them in the context of what was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll do that. But before we do, let's just have a look at English pages 8 to 10 and B/C/S pages 15 onwards of this document to reinforce this particular point. Thank you. I'm not going to invite you to read entirely Chapter 3, but you can see that it's a chapter that describes the procedures for implementing hygiene and sanitation measures in battlefields during combat operations. And in particular, I invite you to look at 84: "During attacks, hygiene and sanitation measures shall be implemented as soon as the situation so allows. Units within the first combat echelon will not always be able to implement hygiene and sanitation measures in the battlefield, in which case it is their duty to inform superior officers that hygiene and sanitation measures have not been implemented." Just quickly, your understanding of the term, did it include, in May 2000, when you wrote your report, the concept of "asanacija" during combat operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I would -- I would read 84 and not see that as inconsistent with my understanding, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So without having seen this document, where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Again, it goes back to my understanding of the definition under the JNA lexicon. Certainly as a practical matter, I agree with the context of paragraph 84, and first echelon units who are engaged in combat are often not going to have the time to implement these measures. That's a practical matter of common sense in some regard. So that's why I'm saying, my reading of paragraph 84 is not consistent with my broader understanding of what that process was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you ever review any VRS document giving instructions for the carrying out of implementation of hygiene and sanitation of the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: At the time of the May 2000 narrative, the OTP did not have in its possession the documents that it now has, which talk about those activities that I believe they're now -- they take place in context of time starting around the 20th of July. I did not have those available to me at the initial reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you seen them since? I'm going to show you 7D481, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe I talked about them in one case or they were on a Prosecution exhibit list. I don't know if I actually talked about them or not. I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, they're not on a Prosecution exhibit list in this case, so I'm going to show you 7D481, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, if I'm wrong, I'm sorry, but can he see this document and can we get on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you insisting on a ruling on that or -- we've had this happening in the past, and we always found a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think we can work it out. I just want to make sure that we're clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there are other documents that you have not indicated previously, Mr. Haynes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't think it's a case of not indicating it. It's on my list of documents for cross-examination. I think the issue between us may well be whether it bears a Defence 65 ter number or a Prosecution 65 ter number. It's really a matter of little consequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. If that is the case and if you agree, I think we can move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can move. It was on my -- there's two of them that were on my list. I can't remember if I pulled them to save time or he spoke about them, but they're clearly -- there's no disagreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move, let's move. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, it does not look familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just describe to us who it's an order from and what it concerns.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: It appears -- like I said, in its initial context, it appears to be an order from the Main Staff on issues relating to clearing up the battlefield, and as was noted, one of the earlier practices that the Drina Corps Command just essentially scratched off some of the header data, rewrote in their own, and it was a document that looks like it would have been disseminated all the way to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, again, under paragraph 1, a description of the duty of virtually every unit, operative and tactical, of the army to carry out clearing up of the battlefield, including gathering and offering first aid to wounded, offering first aid to wounded and sick animals, gathering (burying or burning) the bodies of the dead, and establishing records, finding and gathering animal corpses or using them, gathering and removing all types of waste dangerous to humans, much in the same terms as the order of the -- as the instructions of the JNA we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, in large terms, it's a reflection of a known military concept that often in modern battlefield environments, disease kills more soldiers than combat does, and these issues reflect the importance that the Main Staff, particularly the medical branch, places on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that during the course of the 15th of July, at Baljkovica, there was or were ceasefires arranged between the column and the forces commanded by Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: On the 15th, no, sir, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wonder whether we could look at P2232, page 13 in the English and page 17 in the B/C/S. I'm very sorry. Of course, I've forgotten that the exhibit has a different 65 ter number in B/C/S. It's 2231. But I think the clerk has found it anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the entry beginning at 1330: "Vuk to Lovac: I talked to Semso." Then there's Djuko: "He wants to negotiate. He wants me to give him the frequency of the Turk who is leading the group." "1345. Vuk spoke to Zukov again and agreed to ceasefire under pretence that they would negotiate later. Then he fired one more round 1 for 1." "Igman to Igman 1 - cease all activities." This is the book of the tactical intercepts operators for the Muslim forces. That indicates that there were negotiations for and in fact a ceasefire on the 15th of July, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: It may have indicated that the individual in question, and I assume in this context we're talking Vuk is Dusko Vukotic, the intelligence officer who's carrying these out, I mean, he may believe that, but that's not the way that the situation played out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Go to the very bottom entry: "Vuk to Ikar to Pavle. I talked to Semso and stopped the activities." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I have to assume that Semso is Semso Muminovic, and again I poll joins for butchering the pronunciation. Again I don't know what -- the context of what he's talking about. I mean, they are obviously talking about the mechanisms of trying to negotiate a ceasefire, but as I again recall, they may have been talking about this over the radio, but that's not what was happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "I talked to Semso (Vuk) and stopped all activities." Mr. Butler, are you not able to construe anything in a way that might be favourable to a defence suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's a misquote. It says "stop the activities," not "all activities."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that not capable, Mr. Butler, of indicating that a ceasefire took place on the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Again, sir, I mean, he may have believed it. I'm just saying that my information of what was happening on the ground reflects that that's not accurate information. I mean, it's not the first time where I've talked about the fact that in intercept information, it's not necessarily uncommon that correspondents who are talking about it don't have the accurate information. There's no corroborating information that I'm aware of that would support this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So you dismiss it as a possibility because of the absence of corroborating information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't dismiss it as a possibility. I hold it open. I'm just noting that I don't have any corroborating information that suggests that there was a -- there was a ceasefire in place that early on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at another document, please, which you won't have seen, I don't believe. It's 7D293. English, page 5; B/C/S, page 6. And the witness will need to look at paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a witness statement made by Dragan Obrenovic, dated February 2004, so it post-dates your departure from the OTP, as I understand it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would have been gone by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I direct your attention to paragraph 20, please. "I think that many Muslims were killed during the fighting and that the corpses had been removed, because we only found about 20 corpses between the 17th and the 19th. The Zvornik Brigade buried these corpses at Motovska Kosa on the 19th or 20th of July, 1995." What Mr. Obrenovic is saying -- well, I better check this with you. Had you read this before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't believe I've read his -- this particular statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What Mr. Obrenovic is saying is that at least the Muslim forces, prior to the 17th of July, had and took the opportunity to remove a lot of their wounded and dead?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, and my understanding is that where they could, they did in fact do that, they carried their dead out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then presumably, you concede that that was something that was open to the VRS side to do during the period prior to the 17th of July, would you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I guess I'm not clear about your question. Are you suggesting that -- I mean, I'm not aware of the VRS, except in maybe one or two instances when soldiers went missing, that the VRS abandoned its dead casualties. My understanding is, for the most part, that as the units withdraw -- withdrew from the lines, they took their dead with them. I don't think there was a large body of missing soldiers that fall into the same context. So I think if I understand your question correctly, you know, the VRS took out its dead as well, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And wounded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I don't believe they've left any wounded behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So during the course of the 15th of July, if they were carrying out those sort of operations, namely, taking their dead or wounded from the battlefield, that would be "asanacija," wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, in the technical sense that we're talking about on that definition, it would. The evacuation of the wounded from the battlefield would qualify as that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll be content with that answer. Can we now have a look, please, at P329. I should say 65 ter P329. And just a few basic question about it. In its original form, it is a handwritten document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And have you troubled to identify the sort of paper it is written on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I don't believe I've done that, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's not paper that has any formality about it, it's the sort of paper that might have just been to hand at the forward command post; that's the sort of thing it is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: That's certainly a fair characterisation, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think you and I will agree that this was something that was dictated to another man and written out on dictation.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in the circumstances as you know them to be, not a document that got, in the circumstances, a great deal of thought; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I would disagree with it. I mean, when you look at the document in its entirety, it reflects what I believe to be a fairly accurate reflection of how Colonel Pandurevic understood the battlefield situation at the time. So, I mean, I can't say that it didn't have a lot of thought. I think the opposite is true. I mean, I think he puts a very clear message out with respect to the situation that he's facing and the problems that he has.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In any review you've given -- I'm sorry. In any review you have given of this document, you have confined your interpretation, haven't you, to paragraphs 4 and 5?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I believe for the purposes of this testimony and others, yes, sir. I mean, the paragraphs that people were concerned about were paragraphs 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So you've lifted them from the context of the document, have you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: When I considered the document in its entirety, no, I didn't lift them out of context. It's just for the discussions -- the larger context, I mean, I will certainly entertain talking about that as much as you want, but most situations, again, the part that people were interested in were those two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, what people were interested in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: When questions would come -- arise from either the Prosecution or other Defence counsel, or in the Krstic case, when the Judges were talking about this. I mean, those were the operative paragraphs. I don't think the issue of the combat situation on the lines, as well as other issues beyond that on offers to negotiate, I mean, I believe I've talked about them, but those obviously weren't the issues of interest in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You would, I assume, concede that apart from the fourth paragraph in the English version, the entirety of this document is written about the military situation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, I -- I disagree, only so much as I believe that the fourth paragraph is part of the military situation as far as Colonel Pandurevic was concerned at the time. It's all part of the military situation, just the same as, you know, the discussion on -- you know, with respect to offers to the opposite commander about issues, I mean as part of the military situation. So I disagree with the characterisation. It's all part of the military situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like now to turn to the interpretation of this document that you gave in your narrative report, please, since we are short of time, and I'd like to conclude this aspect today. And that's P685 at page 101 in English and page 106 in B/C/S. And I want to focus your attention, please, on paragraph 13.12. And, really, you can begin eight lines up from the bottom of that paragraph with the sentence that begins: "Later that same day ...," and you can read it over to yourself. Firstly, can we just satisfy ourselves that you are talking, in that interpretation of this document, about the interim combat report of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would you like a hard copy alongside you while I go through this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: I guess if it adds to clarity, yes, sir, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then I'll give you one. You agreed with me earlier, I think, that the use of quotation marks was intended to -- in your report, was intended to reflect/direct attribution to a source; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And for example, you attribute certain words to Colonel Beara, "we'll see what," and you put in square brackets because presumably the word "here" is not there, "he can do." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, again, in this report you note that Colonel Pandurevic noted that there were a large number of prisoners distributed in schools in the brigade area. And we'll find that phrase in your report, won't we?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The next phrase in quotation marks: "Security operations," do we find that in the report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Obligations of security. It is not a literal translation. I agree, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, why have you put the phrase "security operations" in quotation marks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: A technical error on my part. I concede your point on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Technical error?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: And I think we can go down further and there will be another one, I'm just looking at it, where it says: "Let the prisoners go." So, yes, those are technical errors. I hope I dealt with them on my testimony in the court, but certainly in this context my default position is always go back to the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you put the phrase "asanacija" in brackets after the words "burying of the bodies"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Again, as part of the issue of clarity on my understanding of what the phrase "asanacija" meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who translated "asanacija" as meaning burying of the bodies for you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Again, that's a -- what I understand that the passage means, and that's what I put it at. We can go over, around and around on the words, but again this is a reflection of my understanding of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So you put "asanacija" in the brackets after the phrase "burying of the bodies" as an indication that that was a proper translation of that Serbian word, did you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed].
utterances.text: Well, no, sir, not as a proper translation, but within the context of when the phrase is used, what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Perhaps this would clarify things in my mind. Looking at the supposedly corresponding B/C/S text, "asanaciji" is also in brackets, and those brackets are preceded by the words "i pokapanju tijela." Can anyone tell me what "i pokapanju tijela" means?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "And the burying of bodies."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So isn't it the case of a literal translation? The question was: Why did you put "asanacija" in brackets. It's in brackets in the original text -- oh, I see. This is a translation of his report. Okay, all right, okay. That explains it, then. All right. Thank you, thank you, Judge Kwon. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.
